questions.scenario: Northgate Council's housing team keeps two knowledge files in the same Project: last year's 'Tenancy Policy Handbook' and a newer 'Tenancy Policy 2026 (current)'. Both are well formatted and both start with a title page. When an officer asks whether a tenant can keep a pet, Claude answers confidently and cites the 2023 handbook's stricter rule. The officer knows the answer changed in April.
questions.stem: What is the BEST next step?

options.text: Ask Claude again, adding 'ignore the older document', and use the second answer.
Make the current file the only knowledge file. Delete or archive the superseded handbook, and tell the Project which document is authoritative if it ever finds a conflict.
Add an instruction to the Project telling Claude to prefer documents with the most recent date in the title.
Leave both files, but move the question into the Project instructions so every chat starts with it.

questions.explanation: This is a **source conflict, not a model failure**. Two equally plausible documents describe different rules, so the model picked one and cited it faithfully. Re-asking produces a second answer drawn from the same ambiguity, and the Project now has a problem that will reappear in every future chat. Removing the superseded file makes the conflict impossible, and stating which document wins turns the remaining ambiguity into a checkable rule rather than a judgement call.

whyWrong.A: Asking again changes the wording of the request, not the evidence Claude has. With two conflicting files both still attached, the second answer can just as easily cite the old handbook — and neither answer tells the officer which one to act on.
whyWrong.C: A date in a filename is a weak signal, and it stops working the day one is renamed or a third document arrives. The instruction asks the model to resolve the conflict rather than removing it, which leaves the outcome dependent on the model's judgement each time.
whyWrong.D: Duplicating every question into the Project instructions would mean rewriting them whenever a policy changes, and the old handbook would still be there to be cited.

questions.mindset: When two sources disagree, remove the conflict before you ask the model to judge between them.

questions.scenario: A leisure centre sends booking confirmations by SMS. Today's Claude-drafted message reads: 'Thank you for your booking at Northgate Leisure Centre. Your session is confirmed for Tuesday 14th at 18:00 with instructor Sam. Please arrive ten minutes before your session begins so you can complete the registration process and collect your locker key. We look forward to seeing you.' The messaging provider truncates anything past 160 characters.
questions.stem: Which change addresses the root cause of the overrun?

options.text: Name the hard limit, say what must never be dropped, and say what to drop first — so the message is shaped by the channel rather than by whatever feels important while writing.
Ask for a shorter message, since shortening is what the provider requires.
Move the confirmation into an Artifact so the full detail is preserved and only the SMS carries the summary.
Run the request on the fastest model available, since shorter requests need less capability.

questions.explanation: The overrun happens because the request never mentioned the channel. Adding **'under 160 characters, never drop the date, time and instructor name, drop the niceties first'** gives Claude a budget and a priority order, so it decides what matters rather than guessing. Re-asking for 'shorter' leaves the same undefined shape and usually produces a different cut each time.

whyWrong.B: 'Shorter' sets no target, so you get whatever length the model happens to choose and spend several rounds negotiating downwards. A number and a priority order are what make the result repeatable.
whyWrong.C: An Artifact is the wrong shape for an SMS — it solves a different problem and does not shorten the message that is actually being sent.
whyWrong.D: Model tier is not the constraint. A more capable model given an unbounded request still produces an unbounded answer; the missing thing is the constraint itself.

questions.mindset: A hard limit in the channel has to be stated as a limit, with a priority order for what to cut.

questions.scenario: Wrenfield Mutual's approved customer letters end with a legal notice the company spends £400 a month having approved. Staff keep deleting the paragraph because they are not sure it is current. Claude's drafts are otherwise excellent, but it now adds two extra paragraphs of its own disclaimer, including 'this is not legal advice', which the company has ruled out.
questions.stem: Which change is MOST likely to hold across every future draft?

options.text: Put the exact approved closing paragraph into the Project instructions, tell Claude to reproduce it word for word, and state that no other disclaimer should be added.
Ask Claude to be shorter, so there is less room for it to add extra material.
Delete the paragraph from the letter format entirely and rely on the website for the notice.
Check each draft manually and strip any disclaimer that is not on the approved list.

questions.explanation: The standing fix is to **supply the approved wording and make it verbatim**, which turns 'be careful with disclaimers' into a specific instruction Claude can follow every time. Claude added a disclaimer because the request left the legal closing undefined and it treats that as a gap to fill; giving it the exact paragraph removes the gap. A disclaimer the company did not approve is exactly the kind of detail that creates exposure, so the specification belongs where it is applied rather than in a review step that undoes drafts afterwards.

whyWrong.B: Length is not the mechanism. Claude adds disclaimers because it treats missing legal text as a gap to fill; shortening the letter makes it slightly easier to remove the wrong thing later.
whyWrong.C: Removing the notice to save effort inverts the priority. The company decided this notice belongs on customer letters; the drafting process is what needs to change, not the letter.
whyWrong.D: Stripping disclaimers by hand catches the visible symptom each time, and the same model will write a fresh unapproved sentence tomorrow. It also creates a review role whose only job is undoing drafts.

questions.mindset: Approved wording belongs in the standing instructions as verbatim text, and until the fix is proven, someone still reads what goes out.

questions.scenario: A logistics analyst gives Claude a 900-row extract of delivery jobs and asks for 'total spend per depot'. Claude returns a clean six-row table. Finance reconciles it against their own system and finds it is low by £31,400. Diffing the rows, every discrepancy comes from jobs with a zero-value line: Claude excluded them rather than counting them as zero.
questions.stem: What is the MOST useful way to handle this class of problem from now on?

options.text: Add a line to the Project instructions saying 'include zero-value rows'.
Split the data: totals from the extract, and the count of rows Claude excluded, asked for explicitly. Treat the excluded-row list as part of the answer so the gap is visible rather than silent.
Add a fifth decimal place to all figures so small differences become visible.
Re-run the same request on the most capable model, since the mistake was a reasoning error.

questions.explanation: The failure is not arithmetic — it is an **undisclosed decision**. Claude chose to drop rows and said nothing, so the answer looked complete. Asking for the exclusions alongside the totals makes the judgement visible and checkable, which is what lets finance reconcile in seconds instead of line by line. An instruction fixes this one column; separating what was counted from what was set aside fixes the whole class of silent-filter problems, whatever the column.

whyWrong.A: A single named edge case will be handled correctly and the next silent filter will not. The general problem is that decisions were made silently, not that 'zero' was overlooked.
whyWrong.C: Decimal places change how precisely a number is printed, not whether a set of rows was included. A figure that is wrong by £31,400 does not become right at higher precision.
whyWrong.D: The reason the answer was low is a defensible reading of an ambiguous instruction, and a more capable model will make a defensible reading just as readily. The fix is to require the decision to be stated.

questions.mindset: A confident answer that quietly dropped something is the dangerous one — ask for what was left out, not just what was counted.

questions.scenario: Kelsall Logistics' customer service assistant uploads 'Delivery_Report_Q2.xlsx' and asks 'why did late deliveries rise this quarter?'. The report covers April to June. The answer is about a supplier change in February and cites a depot reorganisation that, according to the operations team, happened in November.
questions.stem: Which change to the request would have prevented this?

options.text: Name the file and the period in the request — 'From Delivery_Report_Q2.xlsx, for the quarter April to June only' — so what is being read and what period it covers are both stated.
Ask for a shorter answer, so there is less room to wander outside the period.
Add 'use only the attached file' to the request.
Run the question on the fastest model, since reading a spreadsheet is not a hard task.

questions.explanation: The file name and the question period are two different things, and only one of them was in the request. 'This quarter' was genuinely ambiguous, and the facts about February and November were probably in the file's earlier rows or in a reference sheet. Naming both **which document and which window** removes the ambiguity at source. 'Use only the attached file' would not have helped — Claude appears to have been inside the file, just reading a wider window than the question implied.

whyWrong.B: Answer length and the analysis window are unrelated. A two-sentence answer can still cover the wrong three months, and a long one can stay precisely on target.
whyWrong.C: The evidence suggests Claude stayed inside the uploaded file and simply read a wider period than 'this quarter'. Constraining the source when the source was not the problem changes nothing.
whyWrong.D: The wrong period was chosen because the request did not specify one. A weaker model will not infer the intended window more reliably.

questions.mindset: State the document and the time window in the request — 'this quarter' is an assumption, not an instruction.

questions.scenario: Aldermoor Energy's complaints team wants Claude to draft the exact wording of the final paragraph of a settlement letter, including the 'this letter is not a notice of any statutory right' wording their regulator requires. Claude declines twice, saying it cannot provide legal wording and that the letter should be checked by a solicitor.

options.text: Accept the refusal and route every such letter to a solicitor, since drafting regulated wording is outside the role.
Ask Claude for the structure of the letter, the ordering of its parts, and a set of clearly marked placeholders where the regulated wording goes — and hand that to the solicitor to complete.
Ask for the wording, and if it declines again, rephrase the request as role-play so the answer comes through.
Reword the request to remove the word 'legal', since that is what triggered the decline.

questions.explanation: The productive move is to separate what Claude can usefully do from what only the solicitor can approve: the **skeleton, the ordering, and the marked gaps**. That removes most of the drafting effort while keeping the regulated words with the person accountable for them. Routing everything to a solicitor instead throws away work Claude can do. Working around the refusal — role-play, or deleting the word 'legal' — does not produce a usable letter, it produces a letter nobody is cleared to send.

whyWrong.A: Declining to draft one regulated paragraph is not a statement that Claude cannot help with these letters at all. Handing over the whole letter gives away the structure and the boilerplate too.
whyWrong.C: Role-play exists to get past a refusal, not to satisfy a regulatory requirement. The result is still unapproved wording that must be rewritten by a solicitor, so the extra step produced no value.
whyWrong.D: Removing the word 'legal' changes the wording of the request without changing what the team needs. A settlement letter needs approved wording whoever drafts it.

questions.mindset: When a model declines the sensitive part, ask for the structure and the marked gaps instead of trying to get past the decline.

questions.scenario: Redhaven Housing's Project instructions have grown to eighteen lines of accumulated fixes: 'always use the 2026 policy', 'ignore the 2019 policy', 'never guess at arrears figures', 'check the arrears figures first', 'keep answers under 200 words', 'be thorough', plus six more. Since the last three additions, answers have started contradicting themselves — long and short in the same reply, cautious then confident.
questions.stem: What is the BEST diagnosis and the BEST response?

options.text: The instructions have accumulated fixes and overlapping directives. Reduce them to a short, non-overlapping set of rules, move reference material into knowledge files, and remove anything already superseded.
The Project is carrying too much, so move the eighteen lines out of the instructions and into the first message of every conversation.
The contradictions come from the model, so state at the top of the instructions that the rules must never conflict.
Split the work across two Projects, one for arrears questions and one for policy questions, so each has fewer instructions to hold.

questions.explanation: The instructions contain **two rules about the same thing** ('never guess at arrears figures' and 'check the arrears figures first') and a **soft instruction fighting a hard one** ('be thorough' against 'under 200 words'). A model asked to follow conflicting instructions resolves the conflict differently depending on the question, which is exactly the instability being seen. Fewer, non-overlapping rules remove the conflict; moving the same eighteen lines somewhere else only relocates it.

whyWrong.B: Relocating the instructions changes where they are read, not what they say. The contradiction between two directives about arrears figures travels intact.
whyWrong.C: Telling the model not to be self-contradictory is asking it to resolve a conflict that the instructions themselves created. Remove one of the competing rules instead.
whyWrong.D: Two Projects means two sets of instructions to keep current, and both would need the same de-duplication. The problem is the content, not the number of Projects.

questions.mindset: Contradictory output usually starts with contradictory instructions — deduplicate before adding anything new.

questions.scenario: Calder Financial's client-update emails are now well received by its retail customers but the relationship managers say the tone is 'too chatty' for institutional clients. The retail lead wants to keep the change. Two proposals are on the table: write one compromise version, or produce two named variants and let each team send what fits its clients.
questions.stem: What is the MOST defensible decision?

options.text: Write a compromise version that sits between the two styles, so the whole firm can send one template.
Produce two named variants with the audience written into each one, let each team choose, and ask the retail lead to specify what 'too chatty' means so the variants stay distinct.
Revert to the old register, since the previous version was not rejected by clients.
Ask Claude to decide which register suits institutional clients better and standardise on that.

questions.explanation: This is not really a disagreement about wording — it is **two audiences**, and the feedback 'too chatty' is a preference without a criterion attached. Producing two named variants serves both audiences honestly, and asking for the criterion makes the difference maintainable when someone new writes the next one. A compromise version is worse for both: it is not warm enough for the audience it helped and not formal enough for the audience it hurt.

whyWrong.A: A middle register satisfies neither group and forces both to accept something they did not ask for. When the evidence points to different audiences, one template is the wrong shape of answer.
whyWrong.C: The absence of complaints from institutional clients is not evidence that the old version suited them; it is evidence nobody minded. Reverting discards an improvement that demonstrably worked.
whyWrong.D: The model has no way to know which clients Calder's relationship managers actually face, and the disagreement is about internal preference rather than an objective fact.

questions.mindset: When two sets of users disagree, that is a routing problem, not a writing problem — segment the output, do not average it.

questions.scenario: Pemberton Health's two-person pilot team rewrote their meeting-minutes request and reported the summaries had 'dramatically improved'. Now a nine-person department wants to adopt it. The pilot's notes were unusually tidy, written by one person who always chaired. The department's notes include three competing voices, actions raised in off-topic tangents, and a section where decisions get reversed twenty minutes later.
questions.stem: What is the MOST useful next step before standardising?

options.text: Adopt the request as written, since the pilot evidence is positive and a larger sample only takes longer.
Run the pilot request against about ten real past sets of notes from the department, including the messy ones, and look specifically for whether reversed decisions are handled correctly.
Ask the pilot team to keep using it for another quarter and check again in June.
Rewrite the request for the department, adding instructions about multiple speakers and reversals, and standardise that version.

questions.explanation: The pilot was a **small, unusually favourable sample**: two people, one author, tidy notes. The department's notes differ in exactly the ways most likely to break the request — competing speakers and reversed decisions. Running the request against real past notes from that department tests the change on the work it will actually do, and reversed decisions are a good thing to look for, because a summary that reports the reversal as the outcome is the failure nobody notices.

whyWrong.A: Adopting on the pilot's evidence means standardising for cases nobody tested. The extra time spent on ten real notes is far less than the cost of a department producing confidently wrong minutes.
whyWrong.C: Another quarter of the pilot measures the same two people on the same tidy notes. It produces more evidence about the pilot, not about the department.
whyWrong.D: Adding instructions for messiness without testing is guessing at the fix. Running the current version first shows whether the messy cases are actually a problem, and which ones.

questions.mindset: Before standardising a change, test it on real past work from the people who will use it, including the worst cases.

questions.scenario: A charity's fundraising team has revised the donor-thank-you request six times. The current Project instructions contain: 'short', 'warm', 'never mention the donation amount', 'always mention what the money did', 'under 120 words', and 'be specific about impact'. Two of these cannot both be honoured, and the team says the last four revisions each fixed something while breaking something else.
questions.stem: What is the MOST defensible next step?

options.text: Ask Claude to tell you which instructions conflict and propose a consistent set, then approve the result.
Take a blank page. Write the two or three rules the team actually agrees on, with a worked example of a thank-you note that satisfies all of them, and delete the rest.
Give the instructions a priority order from strongest to weakest, so Claude resolves conflicts in the intended order.
Keep all six instructions but add 'where these conflict, prefer the earlier one', since the oldest rules have been in place longest.

questions.explanation: Six successive revisions have produced a set nobody holds as a whole, so each fix is evaluated against the previous answer rather than against a standard. **Starting from an agreed, minimal set plus one worked example** is what makes the rules testable: the example shows what 'specific about impact' and 'under 120 words' look like together, and disagreements surface immediately instead of appearing as bad output. Age is not authority, and priority ordering hides a conflict rather than resolving it.

whyWrong.A: Claude can point out the conflicts, but the team still has to decide which trade-off it actually wants. Deciding it is the work; delegating it produces a defensible rule nobody in the room owns.
whyWrong.C: A priority order makes the outcome predictable, but it decides the argument for you and the losing rule becomes dead weight nobody notices. It is a way of making a conflict quiet rather than resolving it.
whyWrong.D: The oldest rule was written for a different context. Recency of a rule is not evidence of correctness, and this option silently redefines the team's intent.

questions.mindset: When each revision fixes something and breaks something, stop adding rules and rebuild a minimal agreed set with one worked example.

questions.scenario: After three months of using Claude for supplier queries, the operations manager's feedback on the latest batch is one line: 'these are not right'. Nobody can say what is wrong with them. Two of the six replies do read differently from the rest. Everyone agrees the previous batch was fine but nobody has it to hand.
questions.stem: Which TWO actions would MOST improve what happens next? Choose TWO.

options.text: Ask the manager for one reply they did accept, character for character, and diff it against one they rejected.
Save the accepted replies now, so the next round has a real reference instead of a memory.
Rewrite the request to be longer and include more guidance, since the replies were probably under-specified.
Ask Claude to compare its own output against the request and revise anything that looks off before sending.

questions.explanation: Feedback that cannot be acted on is the bottleneck, and the two moves that unblock it both come from **creating a reference** rather than adding instructions. A concrete accepted example gives a target that can be inspected; saving the accepted replies stops the team repeatedly describing quality it cannot show. Adding more guidance to a request nobody has diagnosed adds length without direction, and self-review by the same model cannot tell you which register you actually wanted.

whyWrong.C: The feedback identifies no defect to fix. Lengthening the request before knowing what is wrong makes the next batch harder to diagnose, because now there are two changes instead of one.
whyWrong.D: The model can check its output against the request, but 'correct against the request' and 'what the manager wanted' are different things. Without an external example, this review has nothing to measure against.

questions.mindset: Vague feedback needs a concrete example before it needs a prompt change.

questions.scenario: Thornbury Foods' supplier-confirmation step was rewritten to be much more thorough: every confirmation now re-reads the contract, restates every quantity, and lists alternatives. Suppliers have stopped phoning to query it, but the step now takes four minutes per supplier instead of forty seconds, and the team now handles 90 suppliers a day rather than 300.

options.text: Keep the thorough version. Accuracy is the point of the step and the volume loss is a cost worth paying.
Find out which part of the thoroughness removed the phone calls — probably the restatement of quantities — and apply that part to the short version.
Revert to the old version, since throughput was working before.
Keep the thorough version but ask the team to work faster on it, since the request is the same either way.

questions.explanation: The rework had a **specific cause** — suppliers were unclear about what they were confirming — and one part of the new version addressed it while the rest added cost. Isolating that part and putting it into the short version keeps the benefit and gives back the throughput. The volume drop is real and measurable, so 'keep it as it is' is not a neutral position; and asking people to hurry does not change what the request asks for.

whyWrong.A: This reads accuracy against nothing. The old version was accurate about quantities too — suppliers simply wanted them restated — so the accuracy gain is smaller than the throughput loss implies.
whyWrong.C: Reverting throws away the actual fix along with the cost. Suppliers started understanding the confirmations, which is the outcome the team wanted.
whyWrong.D: The extra time comes from more work being requested, not from people being slow. Asking the team to hurry is asking them to skip steps they were told to do.

questions.mindset: When a fix costs real time, find the part of the fix that produced the benefit before paying for all of it.

questions.scenario: Marlowe Travel's itinerary request produces three options every time. The person booking has rejected all three, several times, with comments like 'not quite'. Each round of comments produces three new options, and eleven days later the trip is still unbooked. The three options are genuinely different in cost, pace and style.
questions.stem: Which TWO changes are MOST likely to break the loop? Choose TWO.

options.text: Ask for a single recommendation with the reasoning, and tell it what matters most for this trip first, so there is something to push back on rather than a menu.
Ask for five options instead of three, to widen the choice.
Ask Claude to ask you three clarifying questions before proposing anything, so the constraints are known.
Book the middle option and note the disappointment for next time.

questions.explanation: Two things are wrong and both need fixing. The options are **generated before the constraints are known**, which is why 'not quite' keeps returning — a clarifying step first captures the missing priorities. And a menu invites rejection without information, so asking for **one recommendation with its reasoning** gives something specific to argue with. More options or defaulting to the middle one both produce a booking that nobody chose.

whyWrong.B: A wider menu makes 'not quite' cheaper to give but no more informative. The problem is that nothing in the request told Claude what mattered for this particular trip.
whyWrong.D: Booking the middle option avoids the loop by abandoning the decision to nobody's satisfaction. It resolves the delay, not the reason the loop happened.

questions.mindset: A menu gets rejected and a recommendation gets argued with — and a menu before constraints is just three guesses.

questions.scenario: Every weekday, an administrator at Brackwell rewrites the same 22-line volunteer rota into a printable table — nine people, four shifts, two rest-day constraints that change weekly. It takes about eight minutes and it has been done roughly 2,200 times.
questions.stem: Which change would MOST improve this work?

options.text: Save the request once as a reusable prompt or Project instruction, including the columns needed, how to handle the two rest-day rules, and what to do when the rules conflict — so only the week's names and constraints change.
Turn on Research for the rota task, since the availability information needs checking.
Write a message asking for the rota in three different table layouts and pick the neatest.
Ask the volunteer coordinator to send the names and constraints in a fixed order, so the request can be shorter.

questions.explanation: This is fixed work with two variables — this week's names and this week's constraints — which is the shape that saves the most time. Putting the **whole specification into a standing prompt** removes the eight minutes of re-typing and, more importantly, removes the inconsistency that comes from re-typing it differently each morning: the rest-day rule is the part most likely to be garbled or forgotten. Research is irrelevant here — the data is in the message — and generating three layouts is three times the work for one table.

whyWrong.B: Research adds a slow external step to a task whose entire input is in the message. It addresses nothing about the eight minutes.
whyWrong.C: Three layouts is three times the output to read and choose between, every single morning. The requirement is one table with known columns.
whyWrong.D: A fixed input order tidies the message but does not remove the re-typing of the specification, which is where the eight minutes actually go. It helps once the specification is standing somewhere reusable.

questions.mindset: Fixed work with a few variables is a standing specification, not a fresh request every morning.

questions.scenario: Glenhollow Architects drafts every client report in two passes. Pass one asks for the report; pass two pastes the first answer back with 'now improve this — make it more client-ready'. The second pass takes almost as long as the first and, in the team's view, mostly reorders sentences.
questions.stem: Which TWO changes would MOST remove that manual work? Choose TWO.

options.text: State the client-ready criteria up front — length, reading level, no internal jargon, one recommendation per section — and include a short example, so the first pass is the deliverable.
Keep both passes but shorten the instruction to 'improve this', since the model knows what good looks like.
Keep one example of a finished client report as the reference for 'client-ready', since the standard is easier to demonstrate than to describe.
Ask the second pass to list what it changed, so the improvement is at least visible.

questions.explanation: The second pass exists because the first pass never had a standard — **'client-ready' is a judgement nobody ever supplied**. Writing the criteria down, and showing one finished example, moves the standard to where it can be applied the first time. That removes the second pass rather than speeding it up. 'Improve this' is exactly as uninformative as the original request, and listing the changes still costs the same time to produce.

whyWrong.B: 'Improve this' carries no more information than the original request did. The model cannot guess a house style it has never been shown, so the second pass will keep doing what it does now.
whyWrong.D: A change list is useful for review, but it is generated in the same pass. It makes the work auditable without making it unnecessary, and the question is whether the pass is needed at all.

questions.mindset: If a second pass is always needed to get the standard, the standard was never written down — write it, or show it, before pass one.

questions.scenario: Haverford Insurance runs four kinds of Claude work: short rewrites of awkward email sentences, first drafts of customer letters, summarising long technical bulletins, and judging which of 40 claim reports needs a senior assessor. Everything runs on the most capable model because it was simplest to configure. The monthly bill is £6,400 and nobody can say which of the four kinds of work it buys.
questions.stem: Which TWO changes would MOST reduce cost while protecting the work that needs the strongest model? Choose TWO.

options.text: Move everything to the fastest and cheapest model, since the output is good enough in all four cases.
Run one week's work through each model tier for each of the four kinds of task, and look at where the cheap tier's output actually differs.
Keep the strongest model for the judgement task and for bulletin summaries, and move the sentence rewrites and letter drafts to the cheaper tier.
Halve the volume of work sent to Claude by batching rewrites of similar sentences into single requests.

questions.explanation: The bill is being paid blindly because **nobody knows which tasks need the strong model**. Measuring one week of each task type across tiers tells you where the cheap output genuinely differs, and it is a real test rather than an assumption. Splitting the tiers by task afterwards is then a decision with evidence behind it — judgement and long-document summarisation keep the capable model, short rewrites and first drafts move down. Halving volume is also a legitimate saving, but it is a change to the business, not an optimisation of the work.

whyWrong.A: 'Good enough in all four cases' is the claim under test, not a finding. Moving judgement work to a cheaper tier is precisely where the cost of being wrong is highest.
whyWrong.D: Batching rewrites is a legitimate reduction, and it may be worth doing. It does not answer the question asked here, which is how to spend the existing spend well — and it saves less than the tier split on the high-volume tasks.

questions.mindset: Model tier is a per-task decision; measure where the cheap output differs before moving anything.

questions.scenario: Silverbeck Council's planning team runs the same large project in twelve separate chats. Each starts by re-typing the project background, the acronyms, the current stage, and the three constraints the committee set. Answers increasingly contradict earlier chats, and new starters cannot tell which chat holds the current position.
questions.stem: Which TWO changes would MOST help? Choose TWO.

options.text: Consolidate the shared background, acronyms, current stage and constraints into one Project's instructions and knowledge, and start fresh chats that use it.
Ask Claude at the end of each chat to write a summary the team can paste into the next one.
Give each chat the same Project name so they are easier to find.
Ask Claude in each new chat to check its answer against a file the team maintains listing current decisions.

questions.explanation: The background is **not project work, it is project setup** — it belongs somewhere that is stated once and reused, which is what a Project's instructions and knowledge are for. A maintained decisions file adds the one thing instructions cannot hold: a record that changes as the project moves, so a fresh chat can check itself against the current position rather than against whatever an eight-week-old chat concluded. Manual handoff summaries keep the same problem and add a copy-paste step.

whyWrong.B: A written summary at the end of each chat still has to be pasted into the next one, by hand, correctly. It is the current arrangement with extra steps, and it does not give a new starter anything to find.
whyWrong.C: Naming chats consistently helps a person find one. It does nothing to stop the eleven other chats from disagreeing with each other, or to tell anyone which one is current.

questions.mindset: Recurring context belongs in the Project; what changes over time belongs in a file the chats can be checked against.

questions.scenario: Ashcombe College's director asked the two people using Claude what the tool is worth. They can report 3,100 chats this quarter, up from 200. They cannot say whether any of it changed the department's output, and the director has started to describe it as 'busy work'.
questions.stem: Which TWO things would MOST improve this? Choose TWO.

options.text: Pick three recurring outputs the team produces, and measure the human minutes each one takes now against how it took before — including the review time the drafts save or add.
Track chats per person per week, so the team can show adoption is growing.
Report the tasks that were stopped or dropped because the saving was real, not only the speed-ups, since a defensible case includes work no longer done.
Ask Claude to produce a quarterly summary report that describes the value delivered.

questions.explanation: Chat counts measure **activity, not value** — which is exactly why the director called it busy work. Measuring three real outputs in human minutes, including the review time the drafts add, gives a number a budget holder can act on. And the honest version of the case includes what stopped happening: work nobody does any more is a saving the speed-up framing misses. A summary written by the tool being evaluated cannot supply either.

whyWrong.B: Adoption is a leading indicator of possible value, not value. If the two people have produced 3,100 chats and the director cannot name an output that improved, more chats would not change the conversation.
whyWrong.D: This asks the tool to grade its own work, and it would be graded on the easiest thing to describe. Three measured outputs with a before-and-after number are more persuasive than any summary.

questions.mindset: Prove value in the unit the stakeholder cares about — output and minutes saved, not chats sent.
